title: Benediction and the Tantum Ergo
hook: a blessing with the monstrance, and a hymn written by Aquinas

segments.voice: Yesterday, the holy hour, and the question in the garden. Your line was watch one hour. How did five minutes without your phone go? Day one hundred forty-one.

At the end of a time of adoration, something changes in the room. Incense rises. The people who've been sitting quietly for an hour stand up and start to sing, in Latin, a slow old melody many of them have known since childhood. The priest puts on a long shawl that covers his hands. He lifts the gold monstrance and turns to face everyone. A bell rings. And instead of the people coming to the Eucharist, it's as if the Eucharist comes to them. Today: Benediction.
screen: `INCENSE RISES.` → `A SLOW LATIN SONG.` → `THE MONSTRANCE TURNS TO YOU.`

segments.voice: Benediction comes from Latin, bene, well, and dicere, to say: a benediction is a blessing, a speaking well. It's the name for the short service that usually closes Eucharistic adoration. Here's its shape. The people sing a hymn, most often the Tantum Ergo. The priest incenses the host. After a prayer, he wraps his hands in the humeral veil, that long shawl, so that it's clear the blessing comes from the Eucharist, not from him. He lifts the monstrance and makes the sign of the cross with it over the people, in silence, while a bell rings. Then the host is returned to the tabernacle. The hymn is worth knowing. Tantum Ergo is the last two verses of a longer hymn, Pange Lingua, written by Thomas Aquinas, the great thirteenth-century theologian, for the new feast of Corpus Christi. Tradition says the Pope asked him to compose the prayers for that feast, and he gave the Church some of its best-loved hymns. It opens: "Tantum ergo Sacramentum veneremur cernui." Roughly: so great a sacrament, let us bow down and worship. Then it says, in effect, that faith fills in where the senses fail: what the eyes can't see, faith supplies. That's a remarkable line from one of history's great minds. Aquinas wrote enormous books of careful reasoning, and near the end of his life he stopped writing, saying that all he'd written seemed like straw compared to what he had seen. Here, in a short hymn, the thinker bows. That's the spirit of Benediction: after the watching, you don't reach for the blessing. You stand still, and it comes to you.
screen: `BENE DICERE: TO SPEAK WELL.` · `THE VEIL, THE SIGN OF THE CROSS.` · `AQUINAS WROTE THE HYMN.` · `FAITH SUPPLIES WHAT EYES CAN'T SEE.` · then, large: `TANTUM ERGO SACRAMENTUM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: receive a blessing without doing anything. Settle, and breathe. Sit or stand still, hands open on your knees or at your sides. Picture the moment the monstrance is lifted toward you, or simply picture a warm light turning your way. You don't earn it, and you don't reach for it. You just stay still and let it come. If you pray, you can bow your head. Later today, find a recording of the Tantum Ergo and listen to it once. The bell holds the time.
Benediction. From the Latin for speaking well. The blessing with the monstrance that closes adoration, sung in with Aquinas's Tantum Ergo. Today's word.
Your line: the blessing comes to you. Today, when something good arrives that you didn't work for, don't explain it away. Just say thank you. Day one hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Benediction usually closes a time of Eucharistic adoration: the people sing the Tantum Ergo, the priest or deacon blesses them with the monstrance in silence while a bell rings, and the host is returned to the tabernacle.

original.note: Latin: so great a sacrament, let us bow down and worship. The opening of Aquinas's hymn.

what it means: a blessing that comes to you: after adoration the priest lifts the monstrance over the people in silence.
what a scholar hears: benedictio, speaking well; the Tantum Ergo is the last two stanzas of Aquinas's Pange Lingua, written for Corpus Christi around 1264.

notes: Latin opening 'Tantum ergo Sacramentum / Veneremur cernui' verified from memory; confirm. The line 'praestet fides supplementum sensuum defectui' is paraphrased, not quoted.
Authorship of the Corpus Christi office by Aquinas at Urban IV's request is traditional and generally accepted, with some scholarly debate. Stated as 'tradition says'. Confirm.
Aquinas's 'straw' remark (December 1273) reported by early biographers; paraphrased. Confirm.
Benediction may be given by a priest or deacon. The script says 'the priest' in the teach for simplicity. Confirm.
